notes.title: Steam Ealy Access release date changed
notes.notes: [p]Hi everyone! We are working very hard to release Multiverse Designer as soon as possible, and we can't wait to put it in your hands and see what amazing creations you come up with. Unfortunately, development has slowed over the last weeks and things aren't at the state that we expected, so we won't be able to meet the original release date of Late Q2.[/p][p][/p][p]We want to reassure you that it isn't a matter of being stuck in any specific roadblock: we just need more time to put the final work in the Early Access version of Multiverse Designer, particularly to implement some rules with Criteria, a painstaking work that takes a lot of our time. Our backers and beta testers can attest to the state of Multiverse Designer, and that the core product is already fully usable. The new expected release date is September; we are confident that Multiverse Designer will be ready for its Early Access release by then. We will let you know the specific date very soon. [/p][p][/p][p]In the meantime, we invite you to join us in our [url="https://discord.gg/gDFHARKSWa"]Discord server[/url], where you can learn more about the development of Multiverse Designer and see our ongoing development efforts.[/p][p] [/p][p]Thanks for your patience and support! [/p]

notes.title: Multiverse Designer will release on Early Access very soon!
notes.notes:
Hi everyone! We’ve got some big news to share with you, so let’s cut to the chase: [b]Multiverse Designer will release on Steam Early Access in Late Q2[/b] – that is, later this quarter! Very soon Multiverse Designer will be open to everyone. 

Now, this does not mean that we consider our virtual tabletop to be finished, or this one to be the version that we promised our backers when we did the Kickstarter campaign. Opening our doors to all users represents a great opportunity to[b] gather some very useful feedback, [/b]test our strengths and limits, and of course potentially get more resources to keep growing Multiverse Designer even more. But [b]we want to assure our backers that this Early Access release does not change our development priorities, [/b]and we will keep working towards the Full Release version of Multiverse Designer as hard as always. 

Mind you, despite acknowledging that there are still features we have to work for us to move on to Full Release (like the anticipated Asset Spawner or more rulesets implemented in Criteria), Multiverse Designer is pretty much feature-complete as it is – in the sense that[b] it is fully usable and stable. The Map Creator is finished,[/b] with almost 10,000 3D assets available for all kinds of settings, from fantasy to sci-fi, modern, cyberpunk, or Victorian. [b]The Cutscene Editor is also finished,[/b] and you can already [b]create and play online games[/b] with your friends in the maps you create (or download from Steam Workshop). 

[previewyoutube=QOENwgF00Yw;full][/previewyoutube]

Criteria is still in development, but [b]we are working to release with the basic D&D 5ed ruleset implemented,[/b] so the system can take care of all the rules-tracking and bookkeeping for you. Other systems will come further down the line (and we know some community members are also working hard to implement their favorite games, such as GURPS!) 

There’s an important detail that we want to explain.[b] Multiverse Designer will release as a free download on Steam, in a limited version[/b] that allows only to join other people’s games as a player, as well as a limited version of the Map Creator and Cutscene Editor with a small number of assets for you to play around. [b]The complete Multiverse Designer, the Game Master edition, [/b]which gives unrestricted access to all assets and allows you to create and direct multiplayer games as a GM, [b]will be a DLC, available as an in-game purchase. [/b]It is the best solution we have found to make Multiverse Designer as accessible and easy to use as possible, without any potential server issues. 

We want to thank you for staying with us all this time; we hope you keep supporting us when we release on Early Access.[b] We can’t wait to see what you are able to do with Multiverse Designer. [/b]We will let you know very soon more details about what we are working on for the next update, which will arrive along with the Early Access release. Until then, happy adventuring!

notes.title: Dev Diary #10: Moving players around and visual effects
notes.notes:
Hi everyone! After a couple of weeks [url=https://steamcommunity.com/app/1068500/guides/]focusing on our Criteria Courses[/url] (which, incidentally, are still undergoing!), we want to focus on something else that we’re working on that is directly related to how you design and organize your campaigns. 

Back when we were doing the Kickstarter campaign, we received many questions about [b]how players would be able to move between maps: [/b]would they have to join some sort of new session? Would GMs have to “teleport” them by hand? We knew those wouldn’t be an option (it would make for a poor gameplay experience), and that there would be a system in place for players to move between one setpiece and the next [b]without needing to have everything in the same (huge) map[/b] – thus saving also resources in terms of computer power. But we hadn’t designed the specific solution yet. Now it’s time to solve that! 

So, up until now, we were using a pawn asset to define the starting player spawn location on a specific map. Our teammate André realized that expanding this functionality would be the simplest and most elegant solution to our problem here, and now[b] you can use this asset to teleport all players who are taking part in an online game,[/b] right to the location of another pawn asset – which can be on the same map or on a completely different one in the same campaign! 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/2202e340394856ee6c2e0928016f00226c31ba75.png[/img]

Making this possible is quite simple:[b] the pawn asset has 4 new properties that deal with the teleport/travel feature. [/b]First is the Place Name, which identifies the place where the players will be transported to. Second you have the Destination Place Map, which tells in which map in the campaign is that pawn asset located. Third comes the Desination Place Name, the name of the pawn asset in said destination: there could be several destinations, for example, a dungeon with several exit points. And finally, you’ve got Travel: when the GM clicks the according button, all players will teleport directly to the correct pawn asset following the previously mentioned properties. 

This seems like a small thing, but it’s [b]way more convenient than having to load the new map and take all players manually to it. [/b] Just tell your players "please go over there" and they'll automatically show up at the new location! We hope this makes planning entire campaigns (with all the jumping between locations and setpieces) much easier. 

We’re not working only on that, though – and we want to end this dev diary with some nice eye candy. Our teammates Bernardo and Eddy are working hard on implementing [b]new visual effects for your magic and that kind of thing[/b]. Nothing we say here will be more spectacular than a few pictures, so here we go!

notes.title: Dev Diary #9: Dice, Weapons, and Effects
notes.notes:
Hi everyone! It’s been an intense week hard at work here at Toopan Games.[b] We continue working on Criteria[/b] ([url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3453607753]don’t forget to check the first entry of the Criteria Course[/url]!), but in parallel, [b]we are working on improving and/or expanding some features of the gaming module. [/b]We’ll go into more detail when all this is ready to be implemented in the next update, but we want to give you a small sneak peek at what will come next to Multiverse Designer.

The first thing we’ve worked on lately seems very simple, but it’s actually very important, as it’s one of the things you’ll do the most when playing: rolling dice! In a nutshell, [b]we’re making our dice roll faster. [/b]We realized (and some of the feedback we received during the Next Fest pointed in this direction too) that it took too long for dice to finish rolling. Funny thing is that our dice rolls aren’t just for show, that is, we don’t produce a random number in the back and then show a dice rolling animation just for show: [b]we’re actually simulating the physics of a dice rolling in order to get better randomness. [/b]Random number generator are never truly random, and use a numeric seed to produce their results, which can have problems further down the line: if you know the seed you can predict its results. To cut a long story short, we’ve improved the rolling simulation so it goes faster. 

We’re also implementing new visuals for spell area effects. Like this!

[i]Here it comes...[/i]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/ab98d78fc0c4cf91ad021b9d42506570f6c97308.jpg[/img]

[i]...and it goes boom! [/i]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/71c8e8f24bb3862c95c89cdea38e2e0dc2a4f536.jpg[/img]

And talking about areas, another thing we’re working on is[b] trigger areas: basically, spaces in the map that trigger a specific effect[/b] when you step into them. Useful for traps, cinematic effects (like a wall crumbling in front of you or a roof collapsing right after you leave a room), reactive spells, and a long list of other cool things to t̶o̶r̶t̶u̶r̶e̶ ̶y̶o̶u̶r̶ ̶p̶l̶a̶y̶e̶r̶s̶ create interesting situations in your adventures. 

Finally, we’re implementing [b]weapon selection for almost all characters[/b] – until now, in the beta your character model had a default weapon and you couldn’t change its visuals: if they were armed with a sword but your character sheet said it was a warhammer, you could change the stats rule-wise, but visually it would still be a sword. To do this, we searched the assets in the game and extracted[b] about 200 weapons and shields [/b] from several of them. Then we created a system where players can choose which weapon will be in each hand. These aren't necessarily medieval gear, as you can see in the pictures  below...

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/e6e128959f292798ff7a07f52587c896a1f673fb.jpg[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/fcea5dd099fc9960b8fea3b572bf8d1bd77a5456.jpg[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/2418e13a3e167bbbfa1c1ac0775f7e90e30120e9.jpg[/img]

And that’s all for today! As always, we invite you to join our community on [url=https://discord.com/invite/CtZ7YQAUum]Discord[/url], wishlist Multiverse Designer on Steam, and follow us on [url=https://www.instagram.com/toopangames/]Instagram[/url] and [url=https://bsky.app/profile/multiversedesigner.bsky.social]Bluesky[/url]. See you in our next update!

notes.title: Criteria Course #1
notes.notes:
Hi everyone! Now that the dust of the Steam Next Fest has settled, it’s time to resume our usual schedule of updating you about what we are working on in Multiverse Designer. Before moving on, though, [b]we want to thank everyone who downloaded the demo[/b] and tinkered with it for a whole month, and of course[b], all the people who wishlisted it on Steam. [/b]The Fest was a massive boost for this project, and we appreciate all the attention, support, and useful feedback that we have received. 

Now, if you have checked, you will have realized that the demo isn’t available anymore – we de-listed it a few days ago, because we’re working on new features and soon it would be outdated. And what are we working on, you are surely asking? Well, there’s some cool stuff about [b]spell effects, trigger areas, and weapon selection, [/b]but we will talk about that at a later date (probably next week). Because this week we will be focusing on something else that we are working on:[b] we have started to implement D&D 5ed rules in Criteria, [/b]so Multiverse Designer can automatize game rules for you – that is, do the bookkeeping of keeping track of things like initiative, HP, skill checks, attacks, spells, resistances…

But the short-term important consequence of this is that[b] we are using these efforts to record an in-depth course on Criteria, [/b]so you all can learn how to use it to implement your own rules (or to tweak the ones that we’re implementing when the time comes). With this course, modders will be able to [b]create and implement whole rulesets [/b](which then can be shared through Steam Workshop!). As an example, we’re posting the first video here, where we explain how to create a character sheet – that is, not how to fill a character sheet, like when you’re rolling a new character, but how to design one from scratch. 

[previewyoutube=mLQb3AkGiHU;full][/previewyoutube]

This is an essential part when implementing the rules of a game – on the one hand, you have all the abstract rules, like “to hit an enemy, throw a dice, add your attack stat, and if it’s higher than the enemy’s armor class, throw the damage of your weapon”. On the other, [b]character sheets give you the information that you need to interact with these rules:[/b] in this example, what’s your attack stat and your damage output, and what’s your enemy’s armor class. 

This Criteria Course will always come in two forms: a step-by-step video tutorial, where we will explain how to do something from start to finish, but without going into the fine detail of every single thing we’re seeing. Then, after we have explained the big picture, we can go into the finer detail of explaining what everything is and does. And we will also keep updating and expanding[b] [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3453614453]a glossary with the definition of every term[/url] that we have mentioned in the tutorials,[/b] which is easier to access for reference and quick searches to refresh your memory further down the road. Sometimes these explanations will be double, giving you the definition of a term within the general context of tabletop RPG as well as its definition within the specific context of Criteria. You’ll understand the format when you see it! We’ve posted the first video here for your reference, but[b] [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3453607753]go to the Steam Guides section[/url] to see the first chapter of our Criteria Course. [/b]

[b]We can’t wait to see what our wonderful community does with Criteria[/b] when it’s fully implemented and documented!

notes.title: February Update is here!
notes.notes:
Hi everyone! We're very happy to report that we just released [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/1068500/view/545601235427786817]the anticipated new update that we recently talked you about[/url]. It's one of the most important updates since we made the beta available to backers: you'll finally be able to[b] play in the maps you have created with Multiverse Designer! [/b]

As we already explained, along with the gameplay module we're implementing[b] the first rules created with Criteria, [/b]although they're still very basic: rolling dice, HP and initiative tracking, movement, basic actions, character sheet editing, up to 20 common skills, and 3 spells. There's lots of work to do in terms of implementing rulesets, but at least now you can play and have the computer do the basic bookkeeping for you. This update also [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/1068500/view/510698874256494070]implements the Character Forge; check out how to access it[/url] in our latest post (and do send us your creations, you can get an extra invite to the beta!) 

As you know, this update also comes with two ready-to-play encounters: a fight against a wyvern (we recorded ourselves playing it, you can watch it [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/1068500/view/510698874256490687]here[/url]) for the duration of the Steam Next Fest; we'll update it to Youtube when it's over). The second fight is against a group of humanoid enemies. We have also implemented [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/1068500/view/517452371461144964]tutorials[/url] to help with the landing -- Multiverse Designer is a powerful tool with many features that can be overwhelming at first, so we hope these tutorials can help with feeling the ropes of our tool. And finally, the Campaigns, a way to create an overall script for an entire module or campaign, as we also explained [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/1068500/view/545601235427786817]here[/url]. 

Along with these new major features, we've also worked on improving stability and quashing some rebellious bugs; you'll see a more detailed changelog below these lines. That's all for today! See you on our [url=https://steamcommunity.com/linkfilter/?u=https%3A%2F%2Fdiscord.gg%2FCtZ7YQAUum]Discord[/url]server -- you can also follow us on [url=https://www.instagram.com/toopangames/]Instagram[/url] and now [url=https://bsky.app/profile/multiversedesigner.bsky.social]Bluesky[/url]. See you in our next update! 

PS: Remember that [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1068500/announcements/detail/517451737842319532]we have sent you the Steam keys[/url] that will unlock your Kickstarter exclusive content further down the road. Please check your inbox and spam folders, and send us a DM through Kickstarter if you can't find them, so we can re-send them to you. Have a nice day!

notes.title: Send us your best creations with the Character Forge!
notes.notes:
Hi everyone! First of all, we want to thank everyone for what’s been an incredible start to this Steam Next Fest. The number of downloads and wishlists has blown away all our expectations, and we have received very positive feedback and very interesting suggestions. [b]We are incredibly grateful for your attention and kind words. [/b]Welcome to everyone who’s discovering Multiverse Designer now – and let’s keep it up, we’ve got 6 days to go! 

Having said that, there is a feature in the demo that we fear might pass under your radar, as we realize only now that it’s a bit too hidden. We’re talking about the [b]Character Forge, which allows you to customize your in-game avatar. [/b]You can try to make it as close to that mental picture you have of your character – or let your imagination go wild and have fun creating the most bizarre characters! To highlight this feature, [b]we want to propose you a creative contest: send us your best creations[/b] through social media ([url=https://www.instagram.com/toopangames/]Instagram[/url] or [url=https://bsky.app/profile/multiversedesigner.bsky.social]Bluesky[/url]), or share it with us on our [url=https://steamcommunity.com/linkfilter/?u=https%3A%2F%2Fdiscord.gg%2FCtZ7YQAUum]Discord[/url]server. The best ones will get[b] an invite for the Multiverse Designer beta.[/b]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/3883a931434c2864d095d5eab10f9fe6c2a1e552.jpg[/img]

So, here’s how you can access the Character Forge. First, in the Main Menu of the demo, click on [b]Avatar [/b]– that allows you to create the character you will use in your games. [b]For now, Avatar creation is tied to a set of Criteria rules: that is,[/b] you create a character for a specific game. We will look into letting you access the Character Forge separately, so you can create a character appearance that you can save as a preset that you can then apply to characters in any game. Once you click on Avatar, you will have to select which Criteria rules you’ll be creating the character for; for now we only have the rules for the two pre-made encounters in the demo, so [b]select Demo [/b]and click the folder icon to proceed. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/5610bb95d03b0d9c50b09e5891ced07055ad83b0.jpg[/img]

Now, when it loads, you have to click in the [b]tool icon[/b] at the left side of the screen, and then in the face that will show up in the [b]upper left corner[/b] (both things highlighted in orange in the screenshot below). That will create a 3D model that you can put in the map. And when you have put the model on the screen, double-click on it and click on the[b] “Change” button[/b] next to the first item “Appearance”. That will open the Character Forge. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/987f58c1bcf623057b68f319ea682be22af33163.jpg[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/3e37d0c983da3ce1ba986754956557c3da0891d0.jpg[/img]

Send us via social media or through our Discord server your best creations![b] Hit us up with your wildest or most bizarre characters,[/b] crazy monsters, and charismatic heroes! We hope you have fun letting your imagination run free in Multiverse Designer. See you soon!

notes.title: New update coming, and Multiverse Designer comes to Steam Next Fest
notes.notes:
Hey everyone! We’re happy to announce that [b]there's a new update coming, and with some very anticipated features. [/b]It’s been a very busy month (you’ll see why), but this update is going to be one of the most important in a good while.

The next update implements gameplay – at last,[b] you will be able to play in the maps you create or download! [/b]It also comes with the first Criteria rules (so Multiverse Designer automatizes some of the bookkeeping and rules for you), although both things are still limited and a work-in-progress. Basically, [b]we have implemented basic D&D-like rules:[/b] rolling dice, HP and initiative tracking, full character sheet editing, basic and special attacks, over 20 common skills (Hide, Spot, and many others) and 3 spells, namely fireball, lightning bolt, and cone of cold. It also includes [b]two ready-to-play encounters – one against a wyvern and a second against humanoid monsters. [/b]And of course, if you want to do the bookkeeping and rules-tracking yourself, you can already play on any map you have created or downloaded.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/663e754a0ed800722a81e2b3e9b540640e280a41.png[/img]

The second new feature that we have implemented is the ability to [b]customize your in-game avatar: that is, you’ll be able to create a character in the Character Forge,[/b] customizing its face and body as well as its character sheet tied to a specific set of rules (because obviously a D&D character sheet is quite different from, say, a sheet for Call of Cthulhu). Players can do this offline at their own pace, and it will be shared with their Game Masters when they connect to an online game. Then, when you play your character model will be the avatar you have created. 

There’s another new feature coming that is meant to make Game Masters’ life easier. We call it Campaigns: basically, it’s [b]a way for GMs to create an overall script of an adventure[/b] (or, well, a whole campaign). When you create a game you decide which ruleset you’ll be using, what maps it will include, what encounters players will face… You can think of it as how a pen-and-paper book presents a campaign: it describes the special rules, the locations, the NPCs… In the case of Multiverse Designer, it can be as simple or as complex as you want – you can set it as a loose guide or as a very detailed script of how the adventure will evolve. 

[b]This new update is expected to drop by the end of this month.[/b] We’re looking forward to seeing your first games on Multiverse Designer! 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/dbc7f86fa93e551f0171a00d5a68114265c465fc.png[/img]

[h3]Multiverse Designer comes to the Steam Next Fest![/h3]

As we just said it’s been particularly busy as of lately, because we didn’t just work on all these new features – [b]we’re also taking part in the upcoming Steam Next Fest,[/b] so we had to work on creating [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1068660/Multiverse_Designer_Demo/]a demo for Multiverse Designer[/url] as well (as you need a free demo to take part in the festival). We didn’t want this opportunity to become a distraction, in the sense of delaying the development and delivery of new features to you backers, so we decided that the easiest course of action would be to make a demo out of the beta version backers have. It will be available for a very short time, though – so [b]if you want to nudge some friends to try Multiverse Designer for free[/b] (and who knows, maybe even play a game with them!), do it fast, because in a month or so we’ll take it down! Mind you, if you want to play online with somebody who’s not a backer, both of you will have to use the demo version. Due to how the Steam backend works, there is no crossplay between different “games” – and for Steam, a game and its demo are different applications. 

And now that we have announced we’ll take part in the Steam Next Fest, we want to ask for your help just one more time. As you know, we’re a small team developing a very big and ambitious tool. We need every bit of promotion, every opportunity under the spotlight if we want Multiverse Designer to grow for many years, even above the original vision of the Kickstarter campaign – and helping us with that is as easy as important: [b]please share our demo and ask your friends to wishlist us on Steam[/b] (if you want to take an extra step or play with some friends, you can download it too!). It’s as simple as that. During the Next Fest, the more people download the demo and wishlist the game, the more publicity Steam gives us; this event can be a make-or-break occasion for any game, much more for a tool such as ours, which let us tell you it’s not easy to promote – there aren’t that many media outlets or influencers who talk about virtual tabletops! So, [b]by spreading the word, you can make a world of a difference – every single download and wishlist counts. [/b]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/200deccaf07d66f0da4210095a03d225c82f37b0.png[/img]

Thanks in advance for your help. See you on our [url=https://steamcommunity.com/linkfilter/?u=https%3A%2F%2Fdiscord.gg%2FCtZ7YQAUum]Discord[/url]server, and make sure to share your creations if you have access to the beta or when you download the demo – we can’t wait to see what you can do with Multiverse Designer!  You can also follow us on [url=https://www.instagram.com/toopangames/]Instagram[/url] and now [url=https://bsky.app/profile/multiversedesigner.bsky.social]Bluesky[/url]. See you in our next update!

notes.title: Dev Diary #8: Tutorials
notes.notes:
Hey everyone! We're working hard on the next update of Multiverse Designer, which will be arriving very soon -- and with some surprises that we cannot reveal yet! But today we are announcing one thing that will surely change your experience using our tool for the better: [b]we're implementing tutorials explaining how to use every feature of Multiverse Designer. [/b]From map to scene creation, hosting or joining a game, and using gameplay features, there will be tutorials available for you to feel the ropes, as you can see in these two screenshots: 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/d598abb3890871c7392a297e25570720d9d018d9.png[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/b09de134ccf9e8e3c0a483b8608226aa1a694b7d.png[/img]

Multiverse Designer is a[b] very deep tool, with lots of features and thousands of assets, and we understand that it can be overwhelming[/b] at first sight; that's why we think that these tutorials will be very important for new users in the long run. Hi everyone! Not long ago, we announced in [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/1068500/view/4490744894194712890]a recent update[/url] that [b]Multiverse Designer would have full Steam Workshop Integration. [/b]Today we want to give you a more detailed view of [b]how it will work[/b] and show the sharing process for each item.

When we started talking internally about the integration, we realized we needed a new user interface for saving and loading content, so we could [b]both share and search online content without leaving Multiverse Designer. [/b]So we revamped every save and load screen, which are now used to access both the local and online Steam Workshop library.

[h3]The New Load Screen[/h3]

These are screenshots from the load map screen, but [b]the basic layout is the same for all kinds of items. [/b]On the left side, we can access the local library; on the right side, the online Steam Workshop library.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/62db8fb1188422d9252deffc944cd4440793643d.png[/img]

The item name and the load button, on the inferior section, only appear when an item is selected.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/1d9c765035b9edfa1cbbfa90fe2d541c09437818.png[/img]

The items displayed in the list are the ones of the current kind (in this case, maps) that exist in the current folder. We can change the current folder by clicking on the “Select folder” button.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/96f4d5059f5e9d8041dd74364201d38f4cdd6dce.png[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/381bceca5180cab7bc25283fafeebe90b3c23a4a.png[/img]

The item name and the load button, on the lower section, only appear when an item is selected, as in the local library – but [b]when a Steam Workshop item is selected, a “More information” button is also displayed,[/b] which will open the selected item page on Steam in a pop-up screen when clicked.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/fc9a6c5217dd7bf16a6db0eb8b0302dc28fd0890.png[/img]

notes.title: Dev Diary #6: Testing gameplay
notes.notes:
[previewyoutube=n6Dr-LhFoI8;full][/previewyoutube]

[i]NOTE: This text is the same that we read in the video, but we figured that, for those of you less video-inclined or who cannot watch with the sound on, it would be useful to post the script as well.[/i]

Hi everyone! As you know, we’ve spent the last couple of months working hard on what we call the gameplay module: basically, [b]developing and implementing all the features needed for you to play your favorite tabletop RPGs[/b] in Multiverse Designer. We are very excited to announce that work is going at a steady pace without any unpleasant surprises; we are starting to do internal test, and we expect we’ll be able to release it to our beta testers very soon.

And by “internal tests” we mean we are playing ourselves, of course! [b]This video is basically a summary of a 1 hour-long session[/b] in which our team of brave adventurers (composed of a tiefling rogue, a dwarf warrior and a human templar)  faced some fearsome enemies – namely two dark templars, a necromancer, and a skeleton. As you know, the core members of the dev team are Brazilian, so the whole exchange is in Portuguese. But in this summary we will explain what’s going on, so you can see how things are advancing. You’ll miss the friendly banter, but we promise that we’ll arrange English sessions in the future!

First thing you’ll surely notice is that this video features a split screen. What you can see here is everyone’s point of view: [b]the big screen is the Game Master’s,[/b] while the smaller ones are from the three players in this test. This way you can see how every player can have a different point of view, moving the camera freely to get a good sense of their surroundings. 

There are different user interface items that you can see on these screens. The line of portraits in the upper section of the screen represent the order of initiative. Then, the icons in the lower section of the screen are the basic User Interface. [b]The GM has more options[/b] available than the players; the first icon allows you to move the camera around, while the exclamation mark shows the properties of the selected character or asset, as well as the character sheet editor – because, yes, [b]you can change things and assets on the fly while you are playing.[/b] The scroll opens the campaign edit window, where you can add or remove players and maps to the campaign, also in real time.

Then you have a button for Dashing, another for Attack, and a final one for Basic Movement – these are available to players as well. Obviously [b]there will be more actions in the future[/b] – everything you can think of: produce or use an item, sneak attacks… this is just a work in progress! In the lower right corner you can see the button for ending your turn, and in the upper right, the time tracker, which can be used to track any unit of time – assaults, minutes, days, or even years.
 
The key thing here is that you will be able to create or adapt the UI of Multiverse Designer using Crieria. Each ruleset we implement will have its own icons and UI, but [b]you can create new action buttons from scratch, choosing an icon from a big library and linking it to a specific action;[/b] or create a new input, like which spell, weapon or skill that button will use, including area spells. Imagine, for instance, that in your campaign the evil guys are a sect of necromancers, and it’s very common to fight against enemies that raise the undead: you can create an icon that automatically makes a bunch of skeletons appear in the map to make your encounters faster. We will also include a basic, rules-agnostic UI with only the most basic things you need to run a game, like rolling dice, track initiative and HP, and move things around in the map.

In this video you'll see how [b]to move a character or NPC you only need to click the point in the map where you want to go;[/b] you can see each enemy’s zone of control (where moving around can cause an attack of opportunity in games such as D&D). Then when you choose the Attack Action a menu lets you choose your weapon, should you have more than one. It throws the dice, calculates if it hits or miss for you, and then roll damage and deducts it from the character’s total HP. You can also open a log that shows every action in detail.

You can also see an attack of opportunity in play: since a character is crossing an enemy’s zone of control,[b] it automatically gives the option to do an attack of opportunity.[/b] You’ll be able to set different things that trigger a reaction – it is, after all, the same underlying logic that operates traps.

A word of warning: everything you see is a work in progress. Your input will be invaluable for us to improve, especially when it comes to user interface – so if you have any comments, feel free to drop your feedback here, or join us in our Discord server. [b]Many animations aren’t implemented yet, either, so everything looks a bit static as of yet. [/b]A second thing we want to stress: the point of the gameplay module is for Multiverse Designer to do all the bookkeeping for you using Criteria, the scripting language we have created to implement and handle game rules.

It’s relatively easy to have a rules-agnostic system where you can just move character models around and throw dice – and [b]you will definitely have the ability to play like that on Multiverse Designer. [/b]But what we want is to make the most out of the capabilities of Criteria, so Multiverse Designer handles character and NPC sheets, changes in stats, damage, temporary status… everything that you can do in advanced virtual tabletops, like Foundry, with a more powerful system to implement new rules of all kinds, from characters to items, spells, weapons or anything you might think of. 

That’s all for today; as always, we invite you to join our community on [url=https://discord.gg/CtZ7YQAUum]Discord[/url], wishlist Multiverse Designer on Steam(this is very important for us!) and follow us on [url=https://www.instagram.com/toopangames/]Instagram[/url] and [url=https://x.com/ToopanGames]Twitter[/url]. See you in our next update!

[b]PS: Friendly reminder to all backers, please redeem your Steam keys,[/b] and if you haven’t seen yours in your inbox, send us a DM through Kickstarter so we can send it to you. Have a nice day!

notes.title: Dev Diary#5: Steam Workshop integration
notes.notes:
Hi everyone! Today we want to discuss a new feature that may not sound particularly exciting, but that in the long run will surely prove to be portentous: [b]Steam Workshop integration.[/b] In a nutshell, this makes sharing Multiverse Designer creations (we’ll expand that later) incredibly easy, automatizing the whole process through Steam.

You won’t even have to close Multiverse Designer to upload or download anything: it will all be stored in the Steam Cloud. So, for example, while you’re creating a map, [b]you can search among all the creations uploaded by the community, [/b]find a building that fits your needs, and download it with a click and place it on your map.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/938ec5a90d431f5b4d282d263e80469b3878be9e.jpg[/img]
[i]You will be able to download all kinds of creations from the community, navigating across different categories to find exactly what you’re looking for[/i]

And [b]what exactly can be shared, [/b]you ask? Here's the full list:

[list]
[*] Maps
[*] Environments (aka textures)
[*] Lights / Map Global Illumination settings 
[*] Faces (for the Character forge, like big noses, tatoos, clothing…)
[*] Character sheets
[*] Avatars (the visual representation of a character + their character sheet)
[*] Criteria rules 
[*] Campaigns
[/list]

We want to stop for a second to highlight the last two. To begin with, it means it will be as easy as it gets to download sets of rules. Multiverse Designer will release with some sets of rules already pre-implemented for you to use, but we expect to implement more in the future – and on top of that, we also expect that [b]some users will create sets of rules with Criteria for their games.[/b] This is great news for everyone, because we cannot possibly cover every single game in the market; that’s where the community steps in, and why [b]having easy-to-use sharing features is important.[/b] Maybe your favorite game is relatively small (compared with titans like D&D) and we haven’t implemented its rules… but there’s someone else who already did, and you can download and use them!

Also, sharing campaigns is a big deal too: an adventure or campaign aren’t just a bunch of maps, but all the NPCs, events, and special rules associated with them. [b]Sharing and downloading ready-to-use full adventures will be a key feature[/b] of Multiverse Designer further down the road.

notes.title: Dev Diary #4: About the gaming module
notes.notes:
Hi everyone! After [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/1068500/view/7373044403851121237]our last update[/url], [b]most of our efforts have been focused on the development of the gaming module[/b] – the part of Multiverse Designer that allows you to play your tabletop roleplaying games in the 3D environment that you create in the map editor (or using pre-created maps, of course). 

And that necessarily means, as we have explained [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/1068500/view/4620217676530960558]before[/url], working on Criteria. For many people, [b]the point of using a virtual tabletop to play TTRPG is to have it do all the bookkeeping[/b] for you – track damage, changes in the stats and inventory, that kind of thing. And that’s what we’ve been working on as of lately. 

Good news is, [b]Criteria already works![/b] It’s incomplete, but some of the most important features are implemented: skill check/roll works, you can access abilities (i.e. “what’s my STR bonus?”), you can see dice results and a log journal with details you can see by hovering the mouse on icons… 

We’re also implementing[b] a test map feature, for DMs to test their maps in advance[/b] (for instance, to see if it’s too small or big for the kind of encounter you’re planning, or to see if you need more escape routes for your Big Bad Evil Guy…). Of course you’ll have to roll for both players and monsters, but we think this will come in handy. Take a look at this new feature in this video! 

[previewyoutube=pr9ln2aRWtw;full][/previewyoutube]

Now, you may ask why we haven’t implemented the ability of online playing, even if it’s just as an interactive 3D map that only allows you to move characters around. The thing is, without getting into too much technical detail, [b]online playing is tied to Criteria and its possibilities.[/b] We don’t create an online environment and then slap Criteria on top of it – that would take twice as long. So we’ve got a lot of moving parts right now – map editor, cutscenes, Criteria… what we have to do (and it’s what we are working on right now) is to[b] glue all these things together [/b]for the gaming module to work. 

Meanwhile, we never stop putting efforts into adding more assets to Multiverse Designer. [b]We have implemented an assets kit called “Atlantis”[/b], and we’re creating a new map with it for you to use. We’ll talk more about it in our next dev blog – meanwhile, here’s this picture as an appetizer… Beautiful, isn’t it?

Hi everyone! Today we’re releasing a new update for the Multiverse Designer beta. As we already explained, for this update we focused mostly on working on the assets, both adding new collections and improving the user experience of the ones already implemented. [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1068500/Multiverse_Designer/]In that previous post[/url] we went into detail about the assets included in this update – [b]mostly for modern settings, but also vehicles[/b] (cars, trucks, and fantasy vehicles like carriages and chariots). 

In this vein, [b]we added highways, military vehicles, and over 100 modern and sci-fi character models, like soldiers.[/b] With all these new assets and our Cutscene Editor you can set a scene where, for instance, players are thrown from a jeep into a bombed highway, sieged by tanks, forcing them to run for their lives to the nearest trench. Talk about an exciting in media res beginning!

[previewyoutube=yGxZDuall4U;full][/previewyoutube]

On top of that, we have reviewed all our previous assets: [b]we have fixed errors in over 2,000 assets such as positioning problems,[/b] windows floating in the air, invisible sides and texture glitches. We have also corrected the size of all the assets so you don’t inadvertently plant streetlights the size of the Empire State Building. The movement algorithm now works correctly, no matter the size of the assets in the map. We reviewed the tags of all the previously implemented objects, and added several new tags, to make it easier for you to find what you’re looking for. 

We also included new foliage objects, a fancy way of calling grass, trees, and bushes that you can now add to the map (so you’re not limited by the flora already present in the level when it spawns).There are also new candle lighting assets, all of them now have fire and turn on and off. On top of that, [b]you can create text assets and place them anywhere on the map,[/b] useful as notes or even descriptions for you to read as the Game Master. For a better user experience, assets now have names that can seen by clicking the I(nfo) button.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/3dca45521426f44519092d3ab8e40f00160c2663.jpg[/img]

And finally (when it comes to assets), [b]you can now import assets or maps created in Multiverse Designer by other users,[/b] importing them in the same place where they were saved. This allows multiple people to work on the same map and then simply import the other person's work and it will be exactly where they put it. Handy, huh? 

And last, but not least…[b] we have created some new maps for you to use[/b] – as inspiration, to copy sections of it for your own maps and games, or directly to place your adventures within its confines. We have created [b]a modern war zone,[/b] for military adventures set from the 20th century to present day; as well as [b]a modern city with classic elements[/b] (think of a European capital). But our two favorites in this update are the [b]Cyberpunk Waterfall[/b] – the largest city we have created so far – and the one we call “A dark and stormy night”: [b]a fantasy/Gothic horror setting[/b] that will be the delight of Ravenloft, Call of Cthulhu and other horror games players.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/96df5103d91eab2b956a53a8d3f59c5d9eab25d8.jpg[/img]

What do you think about all these new assets? When you start using them in Multiverse Designer, please spare a minute to [b]send us your creations through [url=https://discord.gg/CtZ7YQAUum]Discord[/url] or our social media[/b] – we can’t wait to see what you do! Also, friendly reminder to all our backers: [b]please redeem your Steam key as soon as you can,[/b] and if you haven’t received yours, send us a DM on Kickstarter or email us to info@toopangames.com. 

In our next post update, we will discuss in more detail what we are working on for the near future. Stay tuned!

Hi everyone! We hope you had a great Summer and you could enjoy some well-deserved vacation. Here at Toopan Games we’ve been hard at work in Multiverse Designer (we did take a few days off to charge our batteries, but we did it in turns to ensure our work would not stop!) [b]It’s time for an update to let you know how the project is going[/b] – but first, we want to tell you something very important…

[h3]Backers, please redeem your Steam keys![/h3]

We have already sent the key to the Multiverse Designer beta to all of you, but roughly [b]only 60% of our backers have redeemed it.[/b] We kindly ask you to redeem it on Steam the sooner the better! It’s not just so that you can start unleashing your creativity: for technical reasons due to some limitations on Steam, once Multiverse Designer releases to the general public it would be more complicated to give you access to everything that you are entitled to as a backer. Of course we will honor our part of the deal no matter what and all backers will get their rewards, but there will be less headaches for everyone involved if you redeem your keys asap. We did send keys to all backers, but [b]if you haven’t seen yours it might have gone to your Spam folder – just send us a DM through Kickstarter,[/b] or email us to info@toopangames.com from the same email of your Kickstarter login, and we’ll send you your key again.

[h3]Assets! Give me more assets![/h3]

That said, let’s see how work in Multiverse Designer is advancing. We’ve been tirelessly implementing more and more assets into Multiverse Designer (which, as explained here, is not as straightforward as it might seem – we have to make sure they are optimized to Nanite). We are actively working to incorporate assets from as many different settings as possible, not just heroic fantasy: it’s really important for us that Multiverse Designer can be used for any RPG you can think of, or to create scenarios for any story you can devise. With that in mind, over the last couple of months [b]we have implemented a lot of modern-world assets: from city streets and highways[/b] to diners, cars, and other vehicles, as well as [b]military outposts and warzones.[/b] Here you have a few screenshots as an example, for stories set in the 20th century or even in the present: a good ole’ American diner, like straight from a painting by Edward Hopper. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/e32c05dada40be398af0b25b0b6745456b8b1f29.jpg[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/cba51e4cc805f419f82e62644859d3056b0237cc.jpg[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/ee1e9de2a0c8c6f873d877ef168739be3fd40f99.jpg[/img]

[b]We're still increasing our collection of fantasy assets,[/b] though, with fantasy city elements and enchanted vehicles. See the bottom of this post for a full list of the latest asset collections we've implemented. 

[h3]Getting there with Criteria[/h3]

But let’s be real here: the next major step for Multiverse Designer is implementing what we call the gaming module, i.e. the ability to play within the setpieces you create in Multiverse Designer. And for that, Criteria is essential: the multiplayer side of things (just being able to connect to a shared map, with each player having the ability to move their models) is relatively simple; [b]the point is to have Multiverse Designer helping with the bookkeeping, rule-tracking, dice-rolling and all that.[/b] Criteria is the script language we use to implement game rules; the whole point of it is to give users the ability to create and implement their own rules, so it’s possible for you to add not just your players’ sheets, but also your own house rules and even whole rulesets from scratch.

During this August we have worked on several new features for Criteria, but the most important one is [b]string parsing: now it can parse (that is, read and interpret) strings from RPG tables,[/b] using them to create virtual fields in XLS tables. If you’re not into coding yourself, this probably sounds like Greek to you (it surely did to me!), so let’s see an example. A string can be something relatively simple, like Hit points = 20d8 + 25; [b]now Criteria can read this and understand that it means that a certain creature has 20 8-sided hit dice plus 25,[/b] and make that calculation to get to its total hit points. It can be something more complex, like "Longsword +2 melee (1d8+1/19-20) or light crossbow +1 ranged (1d8/19-20)”. Then it can use that information to create its own tables for internal use.

This sounds trivial, but it’s actually very important: pen-and-paper RPG usually have a lot of tables with unformatted written text that needs understanding before using it in rules; with this string parsing feature, [b]Criteria will be able to interpret these tables and convert it into rules it can use, without you having to manually introduce all of them.[/b] The next step will be creating action buttons for players and GMs based on these rules.

That’s all for today’s update, but next week we’ll dive deeper into Criteria, how it’s growing and evolving, and the next steps we’re taking for the gaming module. Just before our goodbyes, a final reminder: [b]please redeem your Steam keys, [/b]and if you haven’t seen yours in your inbox, send us a DM through Kickstarter so we can send it to you. Have a nice day!

notes.title: Dev Diary #3 Interactive buildings
notes.notes:
Hi folks! As every Friday, we want to give you[b] a sneak peek at what we are doing right now in the development of Multiverse Designer.[/b] This week we got a lot of new assets that we’ll be putting into the level editor very soon, and they all have something in common… but we’ll get to that in just a few lines; let’s talk about something else before, for context.

During the Kickstarter campaign, and particularly during the livestreams, we got a specific question very often: would players be able to enter the buildings? The answer to that is “yes, but only some” – [b]there are assets that are just the front of a building, but are empty inside,[/b] and you cannot actually enter them; they’re basically props. Others have functioning front doors, and inside got rooms, several stories, stairs – everything you expect in, well, a building. Thus, when you design a city, town or whatever, you’re supposed to make interactive only the buildings that are important to the story, while the rest are just there for the looks.

You might think, “but I want to design a whole town full of buildings that you can explore!”. But there is a reason to do it this way: performance. Think of it: when you’re designing an adventure in a city,[b] do you actually sit down to decide what’s inside every single building of it?[/b] Probably not, because that would take hundreds of hours. You design the important places (maybe a few extra random houses in case your players go rogue) and that’s it. If things go off the script so much that you run out of pre-defined resources, either you invent them on the fly or just tell your players “look, that place is not relevant to the story, stop trying to get into random places or I’ll just go grab the Trivial Pursuit from the attic”.

Well, it’s kind of the same with your computer. A building that is fully interactive means millions of polygons, physics calculations and many other things that your computer has to take care of. A whole town where you can enter and explore every building?[b] Best case scenario, your game would be laggy and stuttering.[/b] If you do want to have different pre-designed buildings at hand in case your players are the kind of murder-hobos roguish characters that enjoy entering random buildings, you can always teleport your players there.

But this whole conversation made us realize that being able to enter buildings was a big thing for you when it comes to immersion, so while the point of “if every building were interactive your computer would catch fire” still stands, we wanted to give you as many architectural options as possible. [b]So this week we got a package of assets with a lot of buildings you can enter and explore. notes.title: Dev Diary #2: Nanite
notes.notes:
Hey everyone! After we released the first beta version of Multiverse Designer, we expected to spend several weeks squashing bugs and fixing technical issues. But the original build was stabler than even we expected, so we could shift our focus from putting out fires to [b]improving the general performance of our software.[/b] In the next dev blogs, we want to explain a little bit what we are doing right now; this first post will focus on the optimization efforts we are undertaking.

The main work we are doing these days is related to [b]optimizing all the assets we have so far in Multiverse Designer to make sure we can enable Nanite[/b] in them. Before we move on to explain how we are doing this, we have to answer the obvious question: what exactly is Nanite? As you may recall, Multiverse Designer uses Unreal Engine; for those of you who aren’t too tech-savvy, UE is a 3D graphics engine, mostly (but not only) used for games. A game engine handles much more than graphics, despite what the average gamer often thinks – it’s a complex software framework with many different features, libraries and support programs. And Nanite is one of the major features of Unreal Engine 5, the latest version of the engine.

To be more specific, Nanite lets developers import high-detailed photographic source material into games, so they don’t have to create new 3D assets from scratch -- which would still need to be optimized, on top of it! For example, [b]without it we wouldn’t be able to use Kitbash3D assets without a significant impact on performance.[/b] A good example of this is [url=https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/multiversedesigner/multiverse-designer/posts/4032092?lang=es]the cyberpunk map we created during the Kickstarter campaign[/url]: many of its assets didn’t have Nanite enabled, and due to that, the map caused crashes – because its 3D assets were eating GPU memory like popcorn! 

[previewyoutube=L2S5riUjcC0;full][/previewyoutube]

So what we are doing right now is going over all the 3D assets we have (which weren’t necessarily created for Unreal Engine) and [b]making the necessary adjustments so they are all compatible with Nanite,[/b] in order to make them available and usable (which also means, let’s not forget it, fully customizable) on Multiverse Designer. This isn’t exactly easy, and considering we’ve got thousands of assets, it can be quite tedious too – so we have developed a tool to analyze them and make the necessary adjustments, revamping the loading system and working with some internal procedures to help bulk change assets into Nanite.

The biggest challenge we are facing is the fact that Nanite -- which allows us to use assets made up of millions of polygons - does not work on transparent objects. Our job is, for example, to take a building that contains 4 million polygons and separate it into two parts,[b] one that has few transparent polygons and the other that has many normal polygons[/b] and apply Nanite to the second. Now multiply this by 5 thousand assets and you will get an idea of what we’re talking about! 

Even so, it’s not a drag and drop thing; it does take some individual checking and tweaking. It takes time, but we’re getting there, and soon we’ll be able to move on to other tasks. The good thing is that making assets fully compatible with Nanite also has the advantage of optimizing GPU memory usage, so when this process is completed Multiverse Designer will also see great improvements in performance.

Mind you, it’s not the only thing we’re doing; in parallel, we are working in Criteria, In the next dev blog, we’ll talk about the current work in Criteria, the system we use to codify and implement TTRPG rules, and [b]the monster/NPC generator we are creating. [/b]See you next week!

notes.title: BEYOND THE DICE #6
notes.notes:
[h2][b]How to create interesting characters[/b][/h2]

When create our characters, we are often overloaded with ideas and options and we can get lost on those for a really long time trying to create something that feels real and of course, in fantasy the limits are almost non-existent and doing something cohesive surely is complicated, considering the abundance of choices we will have to make in our sheet, for that reason we decided to share [b]some tips [/b]we use to create our characters!

Before thinking about physical appearance and personality, It might be interesting to think about where the character came from, how was he raised? Who were their ancestors and how did they treat you? Thinking about relatives, not only parents, but brothers, uncles, cousins or other distant relatives they can [b]help you to know your character better[/b], giving them a connection and understanding why they think the way they do.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/8907623db3c7075450438ae1304deb69525011cf.png[/img]


When we establish a place where we come from, we can then think about the personality of the character and  what will be his appearance; he may have come from a cold and rigid environment or he may have come from a warm and joyful land, the type of environment usually is related to the weather  and it can change the character since[b] the general ambiance comes from it[/b]. He could come from  a place with few resources and low food quality, it is very likely that the population is poorer and has to fight to survive, so it may have a more aggressive nature, or on the opposite, if he comes from a region with more abundance he can be someone quieter who is not prone to battles but to work things out in dialogue and have huge convince power. 


While you are creating the personality you shoud also think about their flaws,[b] everyone has desires and everyone has something to fear[/b] these are the two fundamental pillars to create a personality for your character; What he wants? Why he wants it? Some family feud, the Legacy of your ancestors or bringing peace back, are some of the most used among players.

It is valid to choose something that will appear in the campaign for your fear, since when this moment occurs you will have the opportunity to roleplay and [b]a great  chance to develop your character [/b]and make him overcome his fears to help the party, arachnophobia, fear of the dark, fear of fire, fear of death, are some of the most interesting examples we can bring.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/0bf57b5db746bd94c5d8316ff4bcc9fd2ac6daec.png[/img]

These details will help to[b] guide your character as he will make his own decisions[/b], instead you doing so, a character who seeks peace possibly comes into contact with people who seek the same and therefore they are most likely to choose the clergy or becoming a paladin to protect the people. A rogue can have a difficult childhood and so decided to steal to survive, or became a murderer out of a thirst for revenge for what happened to his kin are some popular, and very used backgrounds.

Even if your character doesn’t have any blood relatives, it doesn’t mean that he doesn’t have any “family”, [b]friends and people that support us are our family in the real world[/b], we can transfer it to the character as well, giving it an extra layer. Don’t forgot that even if you character is a lone wolf he will meet other persons in the world before starts the campaign, and even if he doesn’t trust them, he at least know them, use this as a setting for you and which type of character he acossiate with.

The most important thing when creating a character is to[b] create someone you can identify with[/b] ,if you mirror someone with feelings, someone with intentions and motivations, keep that in mind when creating your character, this will make your roleplay a lot easier and your affection over it just grow , these are just a few tips that can be used when creating your character, maybe try some of them and see the improvement yourself and don't forget to tell us what you think!

[i]Good Rolls and See ya'll soon! [/i]

notes.title: BEYOND THE DICE #5
notes.notes:
[h2]5 tips to trigger the feeling of discovery though exploration[/h2]

Sometimes giving your players a feeling of surprise can be a bit tricky and bringing that shiver down the spine before a battle can help with immersion, since the player will focus more and it will make players more engaged in the situation and therefore act better in the scenes.

This isn’t a quick task to do and the DM can be busy at times, thinking through the details of clues to lead something at the end of your campaign can be a bit of a chore and this process  must be done continuously as the story progresses; After all, the master is never quite sure what his players will do, since more than one mind is involved in this process, so we decided to give some tips that can help in these moments, this is our 5 picks:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/8907623db3c7075450438ae1304deb69525011cf.png[/img]

[h3][b]1: Planning Ahead![/b][/h3]
To create a good discovery, we need to plan things out in advance and keep in mind what comes next. Thinking about details is not very necessary at the moment but thinking about the environment and the bigger picture can come in handy as we can plant the seeds of what will come later, tips and clues about the discoveries ahead, we can also use resources such as figures of speech or even the perception of characters using different points of view to deliver different information.

[h3][b]2: Misleading[/b][/h3]
It's not wrong to guide player to dead ends or make them lose the track with wrong clues but be careful as this can create false expectations for them. Facts that won't happen can be a way to mislead players this way but can also create a feeling of frustration in them.

[h3][b]3: Loose interpretations[/b][/h3]
They can be a good tool when creating this type of interaction since interpretation is something that the players will have to do themselves. delivering a prophecy to them in which the meanings are ambiguous and blur can be something interesting since they took their own opinions  from the facts given in the “prophecy” and it may also not be perfectly correct or completely literal  may it be a subjective things such as a symbology for the character, referring to it in a figurative  way using this tricks, you will bring an air of mystery to them.

[h3][b]4: Foreshadowing[/b][/h3]
Foreshadowing is also a very important tool to give, false clues and mislead are just as important as clues that led them to the right conclusion and will make the discovery be based on something and not something out ouf nowhere. Foreshadowing should at first glance be something insignificant or unimportant something that can be ignored or go unnoticed. A good example of this is “A Song of Ice and Fire”, by George R.R. Martin, when a direwolf(Symbol of the house Stark) was killed by a Stag (Symbol of house Baratheon) and leaving their cubs alone in the world, and it happened in the history.

[h3][b]5: Plot Twists[/b][/h3]
Work with Plot Twist! Sometimes the villain of your campaign doesn't need to be the one in the prophecy, it can be the person that leads to the BBEG. Subverting the expectations of the players can be used in these moments players can pass the entire journey thinking and wonderig if  that NPC can be the villain, while in fact they were being manipulated and being used by the so-called “good guys”. These devices are well known so pondering them must be something essential since the same plot Twist will not be so effective the second time you use it.

Remember not to do anything too complicated as your players should be able to figure out the things alone and it's ok if one or two theorize on the right thing, but if you are thinking that they know all of your plans, bringing elements that can get them confused or even wrong! After all, this kind of situation can guide them further away from the main situation! We hope that now you will be able to create your own discoveries and increase the feeling of exploration in your campaigns and this helps with the fun for everyone at your table!

Good rolls and see you all soon!

[h3]Factors to consider when defining the size of every room[/h3]
Every GM who makes their own maps had faced the situation of creating new rooms and environments for their players to venture into, but often this causes discomfort or confusion, some of them seem little strange or a certain feeling that that is not right, so we decided to[b] share tips with you![/b]

Room sizes can range from a broom closet to even a grand palace hall, but you don't see apartment-sized broom closets out there and the reason is that [b]every room has a purpose[/b], a reason why it makes sense and justify its size. As a game master you must think about the context of the room and for what purpose it is used, a dining room makes more sense next to a kitchen than after a bedroom, have you ever imagined the idea of your guests passing through your bedroom before leaving?! Doesn’t make sense.

A factor to consider is the size of the rooms, whether they are small or huge the rooms they must have some logic behind them and must respect the external size and proportion of the adjacent ones, n[b]o room can be bigger than its outside well, not without magic at least. [/b]It's worth to thinking awhile about the use of that space, if it's a dining room or a kitchen that had a big table, the place should be big enough to accommodate all the characters, they have to walk through and give more space for the characters to interact, even more in a place where a possible combat can occur, since several characters will pass and will interact with the objects and each other.

Combat is always a factor to think about since it is one of the biggest reasons for making a map, of course there is all types of maps with every type of function, but it is a really important factor and it actually helps the immersion in the battle time.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/69195003d01f6bd7918ab392cc6c03950c990d9f.png[/img]
[b][h3]SMALL[/h3][/b]
These rooms are more complicated when it comes to creation, given their tight spaces or the lack to space to place objects or furniture, letting the “empty” feeling. This type of room is [b]good for hiding traps [/b]since it has only one path to keep it on.
If you prefer a more open play style, you can introduce other rooms leaving more open possibilities at the dungeon. These rooms range from 2x2 tiles to 4x4 tiles and are perfect for closets, hallways, cells and secret passageways.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/5d11aef9a02cdf5616930c0836101e7e11321c3c.png[/img]
[b][h3]AVERAGE[/h3][/b]
The average ones generally range from 5x5 to 7x7 tiles, these are the best for environments with some furniture, as they have space for you to place objects, they make good bedrooms, kitchens, ritual rooms, treasure room among many other rooms. Is good to [b]keep in mind that size usually comes related to the size of the creatures that live there[/b], an “average” can be “small” if a creature is huge or colossal, or it can end up being a little too big for fairies and imps.
Battles in this room will still be a problem for mobility, due to the amount of objects in the place mobility can be compromised and friend fire can occur, in the other hand this can be a facilitator for creative players, as they can use the furniture or objects to their advantage.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/43e7f77e378e6ce9db9c2e66e09e74c42c6d463e.png[/img]
[h3]HUGE[/h3]
Huge places can be as much of a problem as the small ones, for different reasons, since the DM will have to spend a lot of time accommodating each thing and having ideas to fill up the place. These maps allow some randomness between players, since they can spread out and do anything far away from each other, maps of size 8x8 or more make good courtyards, castle halls, throne rooms, tavern or ballrooms. [b]They also have a sense of grandeur and majesty, but if not furnished well they can transmit a sense of emptiness.[/b]


Every type of room has its function, just have a little balance and creativity and things should go naturally and [b]remember that there is no right or wrong[/b] and each situation will require you to change your strategy, after all you must follow your instincts and make the place as you imagine.

[i]Good rolls and we see you all soon! [/i]

notes.title: BEYOND THE DICE #3
notes.notes:
[b][h1]First steps to create an original scenario for your campaign.[/h1][/b]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/fa51a364e9517eda243a847b41b3de6a288de43a.png[/img]
World Building is a complex process and can easily be [b]overwhelming for both the players and the GM[/b], who inhabits the place, what type of vegetation and biomes, what the politics and society are like, these are questions that will come up when we talk about this subject, which can leave many lost and confused, so we will give you that support in this regard! 
 
Well, maybe the best place to start is at the beginning, and when I say beginning, I mean at the beginning of, well, everything! The best place to start creating a scenario is from the void that precedes creation, instead of thinking about all the cities and their minutiae, try to[b] start with the simple things.[/b] Where did everything originate from and what are its aspects, what religions were formed from it; or in the case of a closer line to evolution, what that process would be, where the ancestors of each race came from?! 
 
Keep in mind that the creation of a world is [b]one part of the development of a story [/b]and there is no problem with loose ends, they will serve to increase development forward. Pay attention to the basic outline at this point and when the time comes the details will fall into their places. 

[h3][b]WHEN & WHERE [/b][/h3]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/e6ac55750d69f80cf48c79da8bc585ea40ff70e7.png[/img]
Every story takes place somewhere but the moment in which it takes place is just as important; think about the place where you live, what was like 300 years ago or in the past millennium and look at it now!  [b]The question of “when” is just as important as the place it is situated.[/b] Think about the type of campaign you would like to have and the themes you would like to address, they will give you a sense of when the story takes place doesn’t make much sense a tribal world with no tech having laser guns and don't be afraid to be inspired by other works or even real life, after all, everything can wake up your creativity. 
 
When we define the central location, we can already decide what the geography, mountains, hills, rivers and vegetation will be like, in addition to all kinds of exotic features, let's say the world you are creating has two suns as an example, maybe because it has more light, the trees have grown more and are greener, and with it bigger dangers hidden among the leaves; it could also be that because it has two suns, the planet has few plants and is extremely arid, difficult to survive with creatures buried in the scorching sands, this just depends in what [b]stories you want to tell. [/b]

Creating a story is easier when treated as one, or several, balls of yarn, each unravelling into something new and often meeting halfway, this way you[b] allow the story to grow naturally[/b] and giving a purpose for each thing to be the way it is, only one choice can generate several reactions and spontaneous creations, this way would be so much easier and will take much less time that it should. 
 [img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/0bf57b5db746bd94c5d8316ff4bcc9fd2ac6daec.png[/img]
We have already established a starting point, a place in time and a place in space, now we need to fill this place with life, after all [b]creatures shape the environment where they live[/b], bringing new interactions, but also new challenges for their creator. How the races arrived at that place they are now?! And why?!, No people remain forever in just one place, giving life to their characters is letting them explore and dream as well, and from their thoughts create myths and legends, they don't need to be real, just the ideas of how each ancestor was seen by that group. 
 
Myths and legends are essential when we talk about a culture, because each one of them has different perspectives and points of view for each situation in their experience so the same experience could let multiple myths about it. Not everything has to be truth since they’re only perspectives and myths tend to grow and change with time, so don't worry about some inconsistencies between them. When creating a society, it is worth thinking about the morality of that people as well as their philosophies and ideals, since[b] society is shaped by its individuals[/b], but how to discover those morals and ideals, political connections or even allies and enemies?! They will come naturally when you develop characters in their stories. 
 
A big decision that you will have to do is about natural laws and what is possible in that world, you will have to [b]find these parameters and set the limits of them[/b] . One of the biggest points to highlight in this topic is about magic and how does it interfere with the mundane, is it easy or difficult to access? Is she banned and frowned upon? Or is it seen as a heavenly gift?! These among other decisions will make your world much more customized and original, even if it takes inspiration from elsewhere. 

In short, don't worry so much, and let things get a little out of hand, sometimes look to your players' backgrounds for inspiration, they can also give you tips on parts of society that you hadn't imagined. Take things naturally and they will progress effortlessly, [b]a decision based on nothing is infinitely more difficult than a decision made with a character's thinking. 
[/b]
Good rolls and we see you all soon!
