notes.title: Beyond the Dice #02
notes.notes:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/f46a5ace2cf5aa19249361e15024c04e38a7fcfa.png[/img]

The vast majority of us have played an RPG where we felt misplaced, whether it's playing a politically focused character in a survival campaign staying years outcasted or a pirate from a Victorian-era playing in an environment where there’s no ships in the horizon; well, I wonder if you have gone through this, if so, I can inform you that there is something to stop these situations and preventing other possible problems,[b] It’s the session zero.[/b]

For those who doesn’t know about it yet, the session zero is a merely chat between GMs and players before the campaign starts, to set the players' expectations in addition to explaining the system rules, the campaign setting and all its singularities such as the house rules, after all, no one wants to play an evil rogue in a campaign full of characters who hate theft, [b]isn't it?[/b]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/6c6ade456df2849c77eb0919e85f1725d41cad5c.png[/img]

This type of session is nothing more than an agreement, where the master will show what he already has done, like the deities of that pantheon, if there is magic or if a dragonborn is accepted in that society or even exists in that scenario after all, [b]there are several worlds and each of them with their peculiarities[/b] and the DMs must let the players know about them since they have the information about the campaign.

The preparation for these situations is a little different from what we usually do in normal sessions, there’s no need for combat grids or even preparing encounters, since in these moments it is advised to have a pleasant conversation with the players and inspire them with ideas and thoughts that could fit into your campaign, but the DM needs a little temperance to not take control of the character, the DM should help giving ideas, it’s up to the player to decide and make the character that way or not.

Another thing to watch out for in your session should be campaign themes and the sub-themes they rely on, such as sexuality, gore, violence, or sensitive topics; [b]we shouldn't make players uncomfortable [/b]without, well at least, letting them know what possible topics would be addressed in that scenario.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/60cd72b07472c5f96d0743877e5a4c5eaeebbb37.png[/img]

[b][h3]ZERO TO HERO[/h3][/b]

[b]What about player preparation?[/b] Well, the Dungeon Master has an important role in session zero, the player is the hole reason everything is happening! The player must contribute with his own ideas, after all, he will be connected with the character for a long time, beyond that, creating a character with personality, thoughts and opinions of his own is a lot of work!

In addition to worrying about your character, one of the problems found among most of the players is that of assumption that everyone has goals or interests close to theirs, but each character has their own motivation and ideal, this doesn’t mean that they’re selfish, but they have their own paths. Asking about the expectations of others or about their playstyles can be mutually beneficial including those who had to answer about it, not only the questioner and of course, there's no need to reveal each character's innermost secrets or their past plot twists, this could be better utilized as a narrative tool. [b]Remember the players make the world as much as Dungeon Master does.[/b]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/7d66399338b531b05805a40db18753b90a886c8c.png[/img]

At session zero most of the GM's work is on planning while the player's is on the future, understanding the expectations of the campaign and his owns as well, thinking through all the details of who he wants to be in this future campaign. The commitment with the table is hugely important, the DMs spend most of their days working or at least thinking in things to implement in the games, players although don’t need to worry as much, but they must have[b] the same responsibility,[/b] so in the session zero make sure to check the schedule since these days there is nothing ending RPG tables earlier than schedule mismatches.

[b]Knowledge and gumption [/b]are the keys in this session! The understand of the players and the DM wishes will get them all in good terms and will proportionate good sessions along the journey, just keep in mind that the biggest reason for the game is fun and this [b]joy is greater when shared![/b] 

[i]Good rolls and we see you all soon![/i]

notes.title: DEVELOPMENT UPDATE
notes.notes:
When you decide to play an RPG campaign, you and all other players are taking part in the creation of an fantastic alternate dimension which in everything is possible. A simulated reality, limited only by imagination.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/f2d0f9222eb486dc8d70d18844cb8bbb9a64f676.png[/img]
Each and every set of rules present in an RPG book was created to simulate reality in this fantasical worlds and rolling the dice is only to help the experience be more immersive. every game has  rules to help with the imersion, but every setting needs has its own rules!

[list]
[*] A horror setting will present rules to keep track of characters’ sanity.
[*] A sci-fi setting will have different rules for lasers, holograms, force fields, or gravity.
[*] A fantasy setting will offer combat rules for melee or ranged weapons, armor, class, and magic.
[/list]

There are countless rules for an ever-growing list of categories.
As soon as we started working on Multiverse Designer, we realized that we want to have all that in the plataform, as much as possible so we envisioned a platform that could simulate all realities.
It was clear to us that Multiverse Designer should be an all-purpose tool capable of hosting any conceivable theme for a role-playing game but how can anyone create a simulation engine for systems that don’t even exist yet?
[u]Sounds ambitious, right? Well, challenge accepted![/u]

[h3][b]THE LAYERS OF CREATION[/b][/h3]
That's when we decided to develop an in-game algorithm that enables players to create and edit any RPG rule they can come up with.
A new language for processing RPG rules was born and its name is Criteria.
Our top priority was to offer players a quick-and-easy way to navigate the main elements present in most role-playing games:

[b][list]
[*] Tables
[/list][/b]
Like it or not, the easiest way to manage the overload of information within any RPG rulebook is through organized spreadsheets. Criteria is a lifesaver when it comes to quick access to attributes, skills, weapons, class, equipment, etc.

[b][list]
[*] Character Sheets
[/list][/b]
An in-depth character sheet with sub-divisions and custom tabs for different needs, such as a list of skills, features or spells. You can add anything relevant (or not) to the characters in your system.


[b][list]
[*] Full game automation
[/list][/b]
We also dislike these long combat scenes that were supposed to last no more than 30 seconds but end up taking half the game’s session. Criteria’s primary purpose is to speed up the game. All you have to do is choose your actions, roll the dice and watch the magic happens.

[b][list]
[*] Easy modding
[/list][/b]
Criteria is flexible enough to allow for easy modding, enabling players to simulate any RPG ever created. Past, present or future.
As we went through with Criteria’s development, we realized the size of the task we decided to undertake. It seemed impossible to come up with something easy to fill but at the same time communicate data and portray narrative. 
To be honest, it wasn’t a simple solution but we’re sure it was one worth the effort and by using tables, we manage that and anyone can edit system data. This means that all it takes to add a new spell, character or weapon is to fill up a spreadsheet row.

We also used spreadsheets to define game rules. With simple yet powerful expressions, you can create restrictions or possibilities for advantages through different game conditions.
The Barbarian class can learn the Rage skill at level 4, or only the Android race can make hyperspace jumps! All the possibilities are endless and you’re in control.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/3db3f3dcb22636cfb32b39b781906aebe078b6b9.png[/img]

This is Criteria’s first layer of depth, which can be easily altered without any programming knowledge at all. We believe most customizations will happen through these simple spreadsheet modifications.
Criteria is a procedural language, partially object-oriented and enacted through a simulated computer inside Multiverse Designer.
That’s right, we had to create a mainframe inside the game with its own memory, commands and everything else, including line by line debugging. Watch out, Visual Studio, we’re coming for you!

[h3][b]Here’s a quick example:[/b][/h3]

If a party of three players is trying to hide from a group of four guards, each player would have to roll a Stealth skill test against each of the guards’ Perception points.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/395e9c340d8370c594ee4da2591444589be2266e.png[/img]

Usually, the poor Game Master would have to compare each one of the players' numbers with each of the guards’. But when using Criteria, it’s easy to automate dice rolling for all kinds of situations.
In the above example, every dice to be rolled would appear directly on players’ screens, ready to determine the outcome of the situation in seconds. At the same time, four dice would instantly show up on the Game Master’s screen, ready to roll for the guards.
Then, Criteria would analyze relevant data from Character Sheets and apply results from everyone’s dice rolling instantly. The spreadsheets are used to execute system rules.
This is Criteria’s second layer of depth. It achieves automation and flexibility within any conceivable rule.
Here is a list of extra features to ease your game’s flow:
[list]
[*] Specific screens and forms for distinct actions.
[*][i]Special attacks, flanking, higher ground, etc.[/i]
[*] Confirmation screen for GMs initiated by player’s request.
[*] [i]Can I roll for diplomacy?[/i]
[*] Extra dice rolling for critical hits with double damage.
[*] All Criteria’s files are available to users, allowing for easy modding.
[*] Add new commands and rules at any time and grow your system as you go!
[*] Additional dice rolling for situations with strict rules, such as invisibility or concealment.
[*] Create your custom calendar with any timeframe for fiction worlds or other planes of reality.
[/list]
The same tools used by Toopan Games to create RPG rules in Multiverse Designer are available to all users. Anyone can easily customize an entire system or create a new one.
Multiverse Designer encourages players to dream high! This is a project directed to the modding community. We want players to share their creations, discover new ideas and be inspired to create.
What multiverses will you design?

Thanks for reading, and stay tuned for more updates! If you want to help us, Wishlist and Follow the game here on Steam -- and let your friends know about it!

notes.title: Understanding Roleplay as a Collective Storytelling
notes.notes:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/d09336f1097415fdecd309ace912849dbfa2c402.png[/img]

Storytelling…  There is power behind this word. 

There are several ways to tell stories. From the ancient tradition of telling stories around a campfire, going through books, short stories, comics, theater plays or movies. 

All those ways have one thing in common: the story flows from the narrator/actors to the audience. Whoever writes a book has total power. Which characters will live, which characters will die and what will happen in the story. This assumption is not true for an rpg adventure

Many RPG adventures are written in the traditional multi-encounter format. Although this makes things easier for the GM, at the same time it imposes an undesirable linearity on the adventure. Let's reflect for a moment: if everything that will happen is predefined, even if the order of the encounters is changed, then there is no story being told but only predefined story that players are obliged to follow. I can see two different approaches to solve this.

[b]A tale of wits: An NPC-oriented story. An experienced GM's solution[/b]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/cadd50589f78a712098060ab97892e8ada8e2be3.png[/img]

The idea is simple: instead of creating a predefined story, start with the npc's. What are their motivations? What do they want? The best NPC's I have created were not bad-bad-bad-bad guys nor are they good-good-good guys. It's good to put flaws in your good npc's and put good behavior in your villains. A cruel villain who battles to save his abducted son is always more interesting than the one who's being evil for money or power.

From the npc´s you could draw places, and *other* npc´s. With that you could sketch what COULD happen but never what WOULD SURELY happen. Create your encounters, but link them to the villain's objectives and be prepared when your heroes turn tail or start digging in the wrong direction. 

Remember that although you're not in control of the story, you ARE in control of the npc's and perhaps more importantly you can always add new places and new npc's to the story - The plot thickens…

A tool like Multiverse Designer is very desirable here in order to be able to create encounters in 1 or 2 minutes instead of flipping through the books.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/3c06abb100c7275b14f89a196125482b616c63e1.png[/img]

[b]A tale of endings: A distant goal oriented story. An easy solution[/b]

The idea here is to create a linear story but instead of planning everything, you just create milestones. For instance:

1) You have this hobbit and a wizard and a cursed ring
2) In the middle he will get aid from the good people of his world in a very beautiful elven palace.  
3) To destroy it he needs to throw this ring into a pool of lava 

What happens in between? YOU DON'T KNOW! Let the player's choose their actions. You always remind them that they´re expected for the (2) meeting and that they have to reach the (3) goal. That's it. Perhaps they will turn gollum into a friend, perhaps they will kill everybody and keep the ring for themselves.Instead of keeping them from doing it, Let them! They will suffer the consequences of course. 

If they're too creative they will force you to be MORE creative. And all of this enriches the story and makes you a better GM.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/496a97e4311e710c36febae7abcc6b32f17cb8ff.png[/img]

Thanks for reading, and stay tuned for more updates! If you want to help us, Wishlist and Follow the game here on Steam -- and let your friends know about it!

notes.title: Using ambience to create atmosphere
notes.notes:
The heavy castle doors open before you, revealing a large room ahead:

[list]
[*]Majestic crimson tiles decorate a straight pathway through the room
[*]The walls were carefully crafted in ancient dwarven architecture
[*]At the other end of the room, an old throne stands tall
[/list]
This throne room was once a magnificent place.

It had been built in the early days of the kingdom that had once stood here, and it was glorious to behold. The throne itself was carved from a single piece of oak and stained dark with age.

The walls were adorned with tapestries and paintings, depicting the deeds of the kings who had ruled here before the last great war came to pass.

But now the place is ruined and the walls are crumbling.

The tapestries are tattered, their colors faded by time and neglect. The paintings are cracked and withered with mold, and most have been torn down by scavengers looking for scrap metal or some other valuable trinket they might find hidden in the dark.

There is no king here anymore.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/eee5fb02d9a9309ef2f1655a42b9db869aaeb2fa.png[/img]

[h3][b]ENVIRONMENT CUSTOMIZATION[/b][/h3]

Experienced Game Masters often take advantage of the environment as a tool for storytelling. During an RPG session, architecture is directly related to character immersion within the plot.

When we started Multiverse Designer we wanted it to be an auxiliary tool for GMs, but we soon realized how important it was to offer a variety of colors, textures, and patterns for buildings and walls.

3D environments without [b]realistic textures[/b] look dull. Repetitive patterns on floors/walls get in the way of immersion and hurt the overall experience.

We understood that to achieve a higher immersion level, we would need to allow for GMs to customize not only the shape of buildings but also the textures on the walls and terrain.

To solve this problem, we came up with a new feature called Environment.

Now Game Masters can create unique environments using an [b]in-game editor[/b] to build anything they might come up with: fancy palaces, stone ruins, marble temples, or ice caves. You name it.

This feature supports an ever-growing library of top-quality textures by [u]Quixel[/u].

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/c2154bb23c3134c61e019626110b6bb44ba2c2c5.gif[/img]

It goes beyond simple editing tools. You can mix different textures to create new ones and fully customize color options like hue, shade, opacity, saturation, adherence to texture, and more.

This type of freedom makes a real difference to create plausible situations and [b]rich scenery[/b]. 

Every time players use a generic Virtual Tabletop to aid them in a game session, they fall prey to a lack of variety in details and the scene looks boring.

We wanted to counter this by giving GMs the ability to build [b]unique settings[/b] to keep players' attention bound to their multiverses.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/a41e077d03099663b1c022f5350a590a2f799bc4.gif[/img]

Let’s not forget that these textures are highly affected by lighting.

Unreal Engine 5 achieves a [b]photorealistic[/b] level of lighting, which opens up a new world of raw potential for storytelling.

A whole new level of immersion is added when Game Masters are mindful of lighting controls in their adventures. Not only to set a thriller [b]ambience[/b] in a dark dungeon but also to create gameplay interactions and mechanics.

By correct use of torches and other lighting sources, the skillful GM could set a wooden chest in a poorly lit room against a wall with the same wooden texture. Depending on character angle or player awareness, the loot chest can be [b]hiding in plain sight[/b].

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/42084beb8eed67c3c40790e6bbee50833954c905.gif[/img]

There are so many good ways of using different shades of lighting to reveal/hide something from your players.

One of our favorite ideas is actually a classic trick. GMs could use a slightly different coloring to draw attention to a specific object. This acts as a visual tip to encourage player exploration and interaction.

A simple wall could easily turn into a secret passageway, if the player is lucky enough during dice throwing.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/e80e695f676e9e2526725cc8bd2f9c5361821051.gif[/img]

notes.title: When dreams become engines
notes.notes:
Welcome adventurer! 

This is the first entry on Multiverse Designer development diary. It all started in March 2020 when we were forced to home office. I always had a dream of building a tool that would allow me to tell the stories I want to tell to my players. Having worked my whole life as a programmer I always had a passion for computer games. However with every game I played, I felt that something was missing. I wanted immersion but in a way that a game cannot provide. I wanted to talk to the NPC's, get to know their fears, their dreams, their ambitions, and that is of course impossible in a computer game environment.

However, this is perfectly possible when playing tabletop roleplaying games! But alas, it leads to a problem: most adventures played in the tables around the world are made up of a small story and lots of combat. If you stop to think about any fantasy movie, combat is important but it never uses more than 15% of the movie's time. What makes a fantasy story interesting is the plot, the characters, their ambitions, what happens in the world and the world itself.

And then there's a trap naturally born in any RPG you play, no matter how much storytelling it has: every RPG needs rules. Without rules, there is no game. Simple rules cause problems and often create unlikely situations because they fail to take details into account. Complex rules also cause problems because you spend hours and hours looking at rules and checking details on something that should have been fixed in a few seconds.

[b]How many times did you spend 3 hours in a combat that takes 30 seconds in game-time?
How many times someone was able to do an impossible action just because a rule is not detailed enough?
[/b]

Cutscene. The year was 1997 and, at the time, I had an RPG translation company. Because of this, I was invited to a product launch party, where I had the opportunity to talk to Mr Dave Arneson for a while and he told me something that I have never forgotten: that he and Mr Gygax never imagined that the rules would be as big as they are now and that the only possible way to go forward with that would be to take those complex rules and run them using computers. 

I then realized that the only way to reconcile the need for complex rules with fun and the little time we have to play is to automate it using a tool. I have been playing as a GM since 1985 and for years, my players and I have tried to use automation tools at the game table but these tools either are simple ordering tools or require you to input player positions and actions and it is impractical to input every action of every character.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42436016/74633446175bdf5b1caf6c58708d360839715a4b.gif[/img]

I wanted a tool that at the same time allowed me to show to them everything that was in my imagination, but also automate the rules of the game. 

It soon became clear that I could build this tool that would use the internet to connect RPG players. It didn't take long for the ideas for a powerful rules engine to emerge, which would be complemented by a world creator with lighting and environment customization, prepared for automated generation, and an editor that would allow the GM to tell his story the way he wanted. as immersive as possible. These ideas ended up becoming the main features of Multiverse Designer, which may look like a video game, but in fact it is a tool, or better yet, a [b]storytelling engine[/b].
